items.prompt: What is calibration?
choices: A private talk where one manager rates a report alone
A meeting where managers compare cases against a shared bar
A survey in which employees score their own manager
items.explanation: Calibration is a cross-manager comparison against a shared bar.

items.prompt: Why do managers compare cases in the same room?
choices: So similar work is judged the same way
So each manager is guaranteed the same number of promotions
So reports can pick whichever rating they prefer most
items.explanation: The comparison keeps standards consistent.

items.prompt: Who weighs in on a case at calibration?
choices: Only the report's own manager
The report, after reading the packet
Several managers, discussing together
items.explanation: It is a group check, not one person's call.

items.prompt: In the unit's scenario, was the engineer in the calibration room?
choices: Yes, they presented their own case
No, they were not there
Only for the final minute
items.explanation: The engineer never saw the discussion, which is why the outcome felt opaque.

items.prompt: What does "rubber stamp" mean here?
choices: An approval given automatically
A careful second review
A rule that blocks all promotions
items.explanation: Calibration is not supposed to be an automatic approval.

items.prompt: What is a "shared bar"?
choices: A separate goal chosen for each person
One manager's private opinion alone
The same standard for everyone
items.explanation: A shared bar is one standard for all cases.

items.prompt: What is a "cycle"?
choices: A person who reviews cases
One single review period
A type of promotion
items.explanation: A cycle is a single review period.

items.prompt: What does "org" mean in this unit?
choices: A department or a larger group
A single job title held by one person
A type of review form used yearly
items.explanation: Org is short for organization: a department or larger group.

items.prompt: A manager argues that calibration is pointless because they know their own reports best. Which answer gives the real reason the meeting exists?
choices: Managers cannot be trusted to write honest cases about their reports, so a group supervises
Each manager's idea of 'excellent' can drift apart, and only a joint comparison reveals it
The meeting lets the reports argue their own cases before several managers at once
Senior managers need a formal way to overrule any decision that they happen to dislike
items.explanation: Knowing a report well does not reveal whether your standard matches other managers'. The joint comparison against a shared bar is what exposes drift.
items.reference:
What calibration is
managers meet together
cases compared with each other
and with one shared bar for each level
Why: a manager judging alone cannot see that their own standard has drifted, so a second check is built in.
items.learnMore:
Calibration as a built-in second check

Several managers put their reports' cases next to each other and against one documented bar. The goal is that similar work is judged the same way whichever team it came from.

Common mistake

Thinking calibration is a rubber stamp that simply confirms what each manager already decided.
items.reflection: Think of a place where several people grade the same kind of work, such as a school or a contest. How do they keep their standards the same?

items.prompt: Two managers each rate a report 'excellent', but one holds a much stricter standard. What does calibration do about this?
choices: It averages the two ratings so that the stricter manager is simply outvoted
It asks each report to choose which manager's standard should apply to them
It drops both cases and waits for the next review period to try again
It places both cases against one documented bar so the gap shows
items.explanation: Placing both cases against one bar shows which evidence meets it, instead of trusting two private scales.

items.prompt: Which description best separates calibration from a rubber stamp?
choices: A rubber stamp reads each case aloud once, then approves them in the order they were received
Cases are compared and questioned, so a manager's decision can actually change
Each manager defends their own report and is never questioned by the others present
Only the cases that managers happen to disagree about are ever discussed in the room
items.explanation: A rubber stamp approves automatically. Calibration only works if cases can be questioned and the result can differ.

items.prompt: A manager says 'I'm pushing for your promo.' What does that tell you?
choices: The manager intends to advocate
The promotion is guaranteed
The packet is already approved
items.explanation: It describes intent, not an outcome.

items.prompt: Was the manager in the scenario lying?
choices: Yes, they never wrote a packet
Yes, they changed their mind quietly
No, they genuinely meant it fully
items.explanation: The statement was honest. The outcome simply was not theirs alone to decide.

items.prompt: Manager support is described as...
choices: Sufficient on its own
Necessary but not sufficient
Irrelevant to the process
items.explanation: It starts a case but cannot finish it.

items.prompt: What is a promotion packet?
choices: The written case submitted
A verbal pitch made in a 1:1
A form the engineer fills in alone
items.explanation: The packet is the written case: accomplishments, scope and impact.

items.prompt: What does the room actually evaluate?
choices: How excited the manager sounds
How long the person has worked there
The packet's written evidence only
items.explanation: Written evidence is what enters the room.

items.prompt: Where does the spoken sentence from the 1:1 stay?
choices: In the packet's first line
In the 1:1 conversation itself
In the leveling rubric
items.explanation: Spoken enthusiasm does not travel into calibration.

items.prompt: Why can't one manager's support settle the result?
choices: Others also read and question it
The manager has no say in the process
The engineer casts the final vote
items.explanation: The case still has to survive a group of reviewers.

items.prompt: What is a "case"?
choices: A legal dispute filed against the company
A list of the person's favorite hobbies
The argument and evidence for a decision
items.explanation: A case is the argument and evidence for a decision such as a promotion.

items.prompt: An engineer hears 'I'm pushing hard for you' and starts planning around a promotion. What is the flaw in that plan?
choices: It treats one manager's intent as the decision of a group they do not control
It assumes the manager will definitely change their mind at some point later
It ignores that managers rarely write anything down about promotion decisions
It forgets that engineers usually hear the result before the meeting is held
items.explanation: The statement is true of intent. The result depends on a group reading a written case, which no single manager controls.
items.reference:
What travels into the room
1:1: spoken support stays behind
packet: written case goes in
room: only the packet is read
Why: support gets a case made, but the case then has to stand on its written evidence.
items.learnMore:
Necessary but not sufficient

Without a manager's advocacy there is usually no packet at all, so support is necessary. But the managers in the room have no relationship with the person, so support alone cannot carry the result.

Common mistake

Hearing 'I'm pushing for you' and treating the promotion as nearly settled.
items.reflection: Recall a time someone promised to put in a good word for you. What still had to happen after the promise for it to matter?

items.prompt: Which sentence correctly describes manager support at calibration?
choices: Support replaces the written case whenever the manager is respected enough in the company
Support matters only after the committee has already finished deciding every case
Support gets the case written, but the case is judged on its own evidence
Support is ignored because managers are never allowed to advocate for anyone
items.explanation: Support is the starting condition. After that, only what is written and checkable carries weight.

items.prompt: After a failed cycle, the engineer says 'my manager must have stopped pushing.' Which fact makes that conclusion unsafe?
choices: Advocacy can be sincere and still lose in a room the manager does not control
Managers cannot withdraw their support once a review cycle has formally started
Managers are not permitted to speak at calibration meetings under any circumstance
A missed promotion always means the packet was submitted after the deadline
items.explanation: A missed promotion does not show a change of heart. The room's outcome has causes outside the manager's effort.

items.prompt: What does "read cold" mean?
choices: Reading it after a long break
Reading it aloud to the group
Reading the case with no background on the person
items.explanation: Reviewers come to the packet without personal context.

items.prompt: A packet is compared against the level's...
choices: Manager's favorite project
The level's documented rubric
Office seating chart
items.explanation: The rubric is the shared bar for the level.

items.prompt: A packet is also compared against...
choices: Other packets for the same slots
Last year's holiday party attendance list
The engineer's own personal self-rating
items.explanation: Cases are compared with each other as well.

items.prompt: Who questions the evidence directly?
choices: Only the engineer who is being reviewed
Only the person who wrote the packet
Other managers with no context
items.explanation: The reviewers are strangers to the work.

items.prompt: Which of these decides the outcome?
choices: How loudly the manager spoke in a 1:1
The packet's written evidence on paper
How much the engineer believes they deserve it
items.explanation: Written evidence is what the room evaluates.

items.prompt: Which does NOT determine the outcome?
choices: The manager's private intent
Evidence against the rubric
Comparison with other packets
items.explanation: Good faith is real but invisible to the room.

items.prompt: Was the manager wrong to say they would push?
choices: Yes, managers should never say anything like that
Yes, the statement was deliberately a lie
Not necessarily; it matched their intent
items.explanation: The mistake is in the inference, not the statement.

items.prompt: What does advocacy mean?
choices: Deciding the promotion all alone
Arguing hard for the promotion itself
Voting on every other person's case
items.explanation: Advocacy is arguing, not controlling the decision.

items.prompt: A reviewer in the room has never worked with the engineer. Which packet line gives that reviewer something to evaluate?
choices: Widely seen as reliable and dependable across the whole team and beyond
Continues to show strong growth and a positive attitude each day
Consistently praised by the manager during regular weekly meetings
Reduced checkout errors from 2.1% to 0.3% after leading the billing migration
items.explanation: Only the first line states a checkable fact. The others describe impressions the reviewer cannot test.

Inside the room
packet read cold by strangers
compared with the level's rubric
compared with other packets
Why: strangers can only judge what is written down, so the written evidence decides.
items.learnMore:
Read cold

The other managers did not attend your 1:1s or see your work. They read the packet without that background and ask direct questions. Specific, checkable claims give them something to answer with.

Common mistake

Assuming reviewers already know the person's work and will fill the gaps in.
items.reflection: When you hand your work to someone who has never met you, what do you have to spell out that a friend would already know?

items.prompt: Two packets clear the rubric equally well. Why might the room still need to compare them?
choices: Rubrics only work when exactly two packets are being read side by side
Both compete for the same bar or slots, so they are weighed together
Comparing packets is how engineers learn what their own scores will be
The room must pick whichever packet happens to be shorter to read
items.explanation: Calibration compares packets with the rubric and with each other, because slots and the shared bar are limited.

items.prompt: What is a slot or budget constraint?
choices: A rule that every case must be rejected
A cap on promotions per cycle
A fee for submitting a packet
items.explanation: It limits count, regardless of case strength.

items.prompt: Can a strong case lose to a cap?
choices: Yes, if cases outnumber the slots
No, strong cases always win a slot
Only if the manager objects loudly
items.explanation: The cap is independent of any one case's quality.

items.prompt: With 6 cases clearing the bar and 4 slots, how many strong cases are blocked?
items.explanation: 6 minus 4 equals 2.

items.prompt: With 5 cases clearing the bar and 5 slots, how many are blocked?
items.explanation: Every case that cleared fits within the slots.

items.prompt: Does a blocked case mean the evidence was weak?
choices: Not necessarily; capacity may be why
Always, weak evidence is the only cause
Only if the packet was written too long
items.explanation: Capacity and quality are separate causes.

items.prompt: What is a good next step after a capped outcome?
choices: Delete the packet
Stop asking questions
Keep the packet and ask about resubmitting
items.explanation: The evidence is still valuable next cycle.

items.prompt: Do two different outcomes ever look the same from outside?
choices: No, they are always clearly labeled
Yes, a capped and a weak case can look identical
Only during the first year of use
items.explanation: Both can end with 'it didn't happen this time'.

items.prompt: If the slot cap rises while the cases stay the same, blocked cases...
choices: Go down
Go up
Stay exactly the same
items.explanation: More room means fewer cases left over.

items.prompt: A cycle has 7 cases that cleared the rubric and 3 slots. Using the assumed numbers, how many strong cases are blocked purely by the cap?
choices: 3 cases, since the cap itself is the number lost
7 cases, since none can be told apart without more data
4 cases, since 7 minus 3 leaves four without a slot
0 cases, since a case that cleared the bar is always approved
items.explanation: Blocked = cases cleared minus slots = 7 - 3 = 4. None of those four did anything wrong.
items.reference:
Cases versus slots (assumed numbers)
6 cases cleared the rubric
4 promotions can be approved
2 strong cases blocked by the cap
Why: a cap limits how many can be approved no matter how strong each case is.
items.learnMore:
A cap is separate from quality

Some cycles allow only a fixed number of promotions for a level or org. When more cases clear the bar than there are slots, the surplus is blocked for capacity, not for weakness.

Common mistake

Concluding that the case failed on merit, when it may have lost only to the cap.
items.reflection: Think of any contest with limited prizes. Have you seen a good entry go without one simply because the prizes ran out?

items.prompt: An engineer's packet cleared the rubric but no promotion happened. Which inference is safest?
choices: The cap may explain it, so ask about the cause instead of assuming
The packet must have contained weak evidence somewhere in the middle
The manager must have stopped advocating during the meeting itself
The rubric must have been changed after the packet was written down
items.explanation: Both a weak case and a capped case end the same way, so asking is safer than guessing.
items.reference:

4 promotions can be approved
2 strong cases blocked by the cap
Why: a cap limits how many can be approved no matter how strong each case is.

items.reflection: Think of any contest with limited prizes. Have you seen a good entry go without one simply because the prizes ran out?

items.prompt: If the cap stays at 4 and the number of cases that clear the bar falls from 6 to 4, what happens to blocked cases?
choices: They stay at two, because the cap always blocks two
They rise to four, because fewer cases means stricter reviewers
They drop to zero, because every cleared case now fits
They cannot be computed without knowing the manager names
items.explanation: Blocked = max(0, cleared - slots). With 4 and 4, the result is 0.

items.prompt: What is an impression?
choices: An opinion without proof
A measured result
A named project
items.explanation: Impressions give a reader nothing to check.

items.prompt: Which claim is checkable?
choices: Has grown a lot this year
Is generally well-liked by everyone
Error rate fell from 2.1% to 0.3%
items.explanation: A before-and-after number can be verified.

items.prompt: What does falsifiable mean?
choices: It is always false by definition
It can be tested as true or false
It cannot ever be written down at all
items.explanation: Falsifiable claims can be tested.

items.prompt: What does the first question in the room usually ask?
choices: Grown compared to what?
What is their favorite tool?
Who hired them?
items.explanation: Strangers ask for specifics.

items.prompt: Which phrase is an impression?
choices: Mentored two engineers who shipped independently
Led a migration across three teams
Strong potential
items.explanation: Potential is an opinion, not evidence.

items.prompt: Why does a stranger need checkable claims?
choices: They dislike the engineer personally
They have no personal context to rely on
They are always in a great hurry
items.explanation: Without context, only checkable facts help.

items.prompt: Which pair is the same work described two ways?
choices: 'High-quality' versus 'error rate 2.1% to 0.3%'
'Error rate 2.1% to 0.3%' versus 'a pizza party'
'Well-liked' versus 'a salary figure'
items.explanation: The rewrite keeps the work and adds evidence.

items.prompt: Does the rewrite claim the engineer did different work?
choices: Yes, it invents new work
Yes, it removes the work
No, only more specifically
items.explanation: Only the checkability changed.

items.prompt: A draft reads 'greatly improved reliability.' Which rewrite is strongest?
choices: Delivered a major reliability improvement that the team strongly valued overall
Cut checkout errors from 2.1% to 0.3% after the phased billing migration
Improved reliability significantly and was recognized for the effort shown
Led reliability work and is trusted to handle difficult problems very well
items.explanation: The first states a number and a project a stranger could check. The others are rephrased impressions.
items.reference:
Impression versus evidence
'grown a lot' : cannot be checked
'2.1% to 0.3%' : can be checked
'well-liked' : cannot be checked
Why: a checkable claim is falsifiable, so a stranger can test it instead of taking it on faith.
items.learnMore:
Falsifiable claims

A claim is checkable if someone could find out whether it is true. Named projects, before-and-after numbers and responsibilities that other people can confirm all qualify. Adjectives alone do not.

Common mistake

Writing 'greatly improved' because it sounds strong, when no stranger can test it.
items.reflection: Think of the last time you had to convince someone who did not know you. Which of your claims could they verify, and which did they have to trust?

items.prompt: Why does the rewritten packet survive a question the draft cannot?
choices: Its writer is more senior and so is believed more easily by reviewers
It is longer, and reviewers read longer packets much more carefully
It avoids numbers, which reviewers usually distrust in written packets
Its claims can be tested, while the draft's can only be believed or doubted
items.explanation: Survival depends on checkability, not on length or the writer's standing.

choices: It sounds more modest, which reviewers tend to prefer in these packets
Another manager could ask those two people and confirm the outcome
It avoids mentioning the engineer, which keeps the whole packet neutral
It is shorter, and reviewers reward brief claims over longer ones
items.explanation: A concrete outcome that others can confirm is checkable. 'Good mentor' is an opinion.

items.prompt: Impact asks...
choices: How long the person has worked there
Who the manager is
What changed because of the work
items.explanation: Impact is about change produced.

items.prompt: Scope asks...
choices: How loud the person is in meetings
How big the responsibility was
What time of day they usually start
items.explanation: Scope is the size of the responsibility.

items.prompt: Ownership asks...
choices: Whether they carried it unprompted
Whether they personally own the laptop
Whether they sit near the manager
items.explanation: Ownership is carrying responsibility unprompted.

items.prompt: Multiplying impact means...
choices: Doing the same task twice
Asking for more slots
Helping others produce better work
items.explanation: It extends beyond the person's own output.

items.prompt: Taking over the on-call redesign after the owner left shows...
choices: Only a lucky guess
Ownership of the work
A reduction in slots
items.explanation: Picking up the work unprompted is ownership.

items.prompt: Two mentees shipping independently shows...
choices: Multiplying impact
A slot constraint
A rubber stamp review
items.explanation: Others became more effective.

items.prompt: Leading a migration across three teams shows...
choices: Calibration
Falsifiability
Scope of the work
items.explanation: Coordinating three teams is a large responsibility.

items.prompt: Are strong numbers alone always enough for the next level?
choices: Yes, in every case
Not by themselves alone
Only if the list is short
items.explanation: Rubrics often ask for more than impact.

items.prompt: A packet lists large error-rate drops but nothing about who drove the work or whom it helped. What is the likely gap?
choices: It shows impact without scope, ownership or multiplying impact
It shows too many numbers, which reviewers always distrust on sight
It shows ownership but hides the results from the reviewers present
It shows no evidence of anything, since numbers are meaningless here
items.explanation: Numbers show impact. A rubric for a bigger role often wants evidence of responsibility and of helping others too.
items.reference:
Four questions a rubric may ask
impact: what changed?
scope: how large was it?
ownership: carried without being driven?
multiplying: did others improve?
Why: numbers alone show impact; many rubrics also want the other three on paper.
items.learnMore:
Beyond impact

A strong result shows impact. Scope shows how big the responsibility was, ownership shows the person carried it unprompted, and multiplying impact shows other people did better work because of them.

Common mistake

Filling the packet with results and leaving out the responsibility behind them.
items.reflection: Think of someone you consider reliable. Beyond what they achieve, how do you know they carry things without being chased?

items.prompt: Which packet line best evidences ownership?
choices: Contributed meaningfully to the on-call redesign alongside the wider team
Was assigned the on-call redesign by the manager during planning
Took over the on-call redesign after the previous owner left unprompted
Is enthusiastic about on-call work and talks about it quite often
items.explanation: Unprompted pickup of abandoned work is the clearest ownership signal. The others show assignment, participation or interest.

items.prompt: An engineer's own output is excellent, but nobody else on the team got better work done through them. Which rubric idea is missing?
choices: Multiplying impact, meaning others' output improving because of them
Falsifiability, meaning the claims in the packet can be tested
Calibration, meaning cases are compared across several managers
Slot capacity, meaning how many promotions one cycle allows
items.explanation: Strong individual work is impact. Multiplying impact is the separate effect on other people.

items.prompt: What do both a capped case and a weak case often hear?
choices: 'You are promoted'
'It didn't happen this time'
'The meeting was cancelled'
items.explanation: The message is the same for different causes.

items.prompt: What question separates the two?
choices: Cleared the bar, or lost to a cap?
What is your favorite work tool?
Who else applied for promotion this time?
items.explanation: That question names both possibilities.

items.prompt: If the case cleared the bar but was capped, the next step is...
choices: Give up on promotions
Rewrite nothing and argue louder
Refresh the evidence and resubmit
items.explanation: A strong case mostly needs patience and resubmission.

items.prompt: If the case did not clear the bar, the next step is...
choices: Wait a cycle with no changes made
Build different, stronger evidence
Ask the committee to add more slots
items.explanation: The case itself needs work.

items.prompt: Why ask instead of guess?
choices: Each needs different next steps
Guessing is not allowed
Managers prefer questions
items.explanation: Wrong guesses mean wrong work.

items.prompt: Who is best placed to answer?
choices: A stranger outside the company
Nobody at all can possibly know
The manager who advocated for you
items.explanation: They saw what happened.

items.prompt: A simple version of the question is...
choices: Why do you dislike me so much?
Was it not ready, or no room?
What is the weather like today?
items.explanation: It names both possible causes.

items.prompt: Does asking blame the manager?
choices: No, it only asks for clarity
Yes, it always assigns blame
Only when it is put in writing
items.explanation: It is a request for information.

items.prompt: An engineer's manager says only 'it didn't happen this time.' Which follow-up gets the most useful answer?
choices: Can you tell me honestly how you feel about my performance overall?
Who else was promoted this cycle, and what did their packets say?
Will you promise to push harder for me during the next cycle?
Did the packet clear the bar and lose to a cap, or was the case not ready?
items.explanation: Only the first question separates the two causes that produce the same vague message.
items.reference:
One question, two paths
cleared the bar, capped: refresh and resubmit
did not clear the bar: build stronger evidence
Why: both outcomes sound identical until you ask which one happened, and each needs different work.
items.learnMore:
Asking directly

'It didn't happen this time' hides two situations. A manager who advocated can often say plainly whether the packet cleared the bar and lost to a cap, or whether it was not ready yet.

Common mistake

Guessing the cause and then working on the wrong thing.
items.reflection: Think of a time you got a vague no. What single question would have told you whether to try again the same way or change approach?

items.prompt: The manager answers: the packet cleared the bar but lost to the cap. What should the engineer do next?
choices: Rebuild the entire packet from scratch using completely different projects
Preserve and refresh the evidence, and ask about resubmitting next cycle
Assume the rubric is unfair and stop pursuing the promotion entirely
Ask the committee to remove the cap for this one particular case
items.explanation: The case was strong, so the work is to keep it current and resubmit, not to rebuild it.

items.prompt: The manager answers: the packet did not clear the bar. Which next step fits?

Gather different, stronger evidence of scope and ownership before the next cycle
items.explanation: A case that fell short needs better evidence. Resubmitting unchanged repeats the failure.
